item.title: Eastern North Pacific Tropical Weather Outlook
item.description:
427
ABPZ20 KNHC 281737
TWOEP

Tropical Weather Outlook
NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL
1100 AM PDT Fri Aug 28 2026

For the eastern and central North Pacific east of 180 longitude:

Active Systems:
The National Hurricane Center is issuing advisories on Tropical
Storm Karina, located well south-southwest of the southern tip of
the Baja California Peninsula, and on Tropical Storm Lowell,
located well east-southeast of the Hawaiian Islands.

Well Offshore of Southwestern Mexico:
An area of low pressure is forecast to form during the next day or
two well to the south of southwestern Mexico. Environmental
conditions appear favorable for gradual development of this system,
and a tropical depression is likely to form early next week while
it moves west-northwestward to northwestward at 10 to 15 mph.
* Formation chance through 48 hours...low...near 0 percent.
* Formation chance through 7 days...high...80 percent.

Central Pacific:
An area of low pressure could form well south or southwest of the
Hawaiian Islands in a few days. Some gradual development is possible
thereafter and a tropical depression could form during the middle
part of next week while the system moves slowly west-northwestward,
well offshore of the Hawaiian Islands.
* Formation chance through 48 hours...low...near 0 percent.
* Formation chance through 7 days...medium...40 percent.

&&
Public Advisories on Tropical Storm Karina are issued under WMO
header WTPZ31 KNHC and under AWIPS header MIATCPEP1.
Forecast/Advisories on Tropical Storm Karina are issued under WMO
header WTPZ21 KNHC and under AWIPS header MIATCMEP1.

Public Advisories on Tropical Storm Lowell are issued under WMO
header WTPZ32 KNHC and under AWIPS header MIATCPEP2.
Forecast/Advisories on Tropical Storm Lowell are issued under WMO
header WTPZ22 KNHC and under AWIPS header MIATCMEP2.

NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL       EP112026
200 PM PDT Fri Aug 28 2026
 
...KARINA STRENGTHENING AND FORECAST TO BECOME A POWERFUL MAJOR 
HURRICANE WELL OFFSHORE OF SOUTHWESTERN MEXICO...
 
 
SUMMARY OF 200 PM PDT...2100 UTC...INFORMATION
----------------------------------------------
LOCATION...13.7N 115.5W
ABOUT 735 MI...1180 KM SSW OF THE SOUTHERN TIP OF BAJA CALIFORNIA
MAXIMUM SUSTAINED WINDS...65 MPH...100 KM/H
PRESENT MOVEMENT...NW OR 315 DEGREES AT 9 MPH...15 KM/H
MINIMUM CENTRAL PRESSURE...990 MB...29.24 INCHES
 
 
WATCHES AND WARNINGS
--------------------
There are no coastal watches or warnings in effect.
 
 
DISCUSSION AND OUTLOOK
----------------------
At 200 PM PDT (2100 UTC), the center of Tropical Storm Karina was
located near latitude 13.7 North, longitude 115.5 West. Karina is
moving toward the northwest near 9 mph (15 km/h), and this
general motion is expected to continue over the next day or so,
followed by a more westward turn.

Satellite wind-data indicate that the maximum sustained winds have 
increased to near 65 mph (100 km/h) with higher gusts. Karina is 
forecast to become a hurricane by early Saturday and could become a 
major hurricane on Sunday. 
 
Tropical-storm-force winds extend outward up to 230 miles (370 km)
from the center.
 
The estimated minimum central pressure is 990 mb (29.24 inches).
 
 
HAZARDS AFFECTING LAND
----------------------
SURF:  Swells generated by Karina will begin to affect portions of
the coast of southwest Mexico and the Baja California Peninsula
this weekend.  These swells are likely to cause life-threatening
surf and rip current conditions. Please consult products from your
local weather office.
 
 
NEXT ADVISORY
-------------
Next complete advisory at 800 PM PDT.
 
$$
Forecaster Blake

item.title: Tropical Storm Karina Forecast Discussion Number 5
item.description:
Issued at 200 PM PDT Fri Aug 28 2026 
000
WTPZ41 KNHC 282031
TCDEP1
 
Tropical Storm Karina Discussion Number   5
NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL       EP112026
200 PM PDT Fri Aug 28 2026

Karina is slowly becoming better organized, with visible satellite 
imagery showing increased spiral banding around a central dense 
overcast. The low-level center is still on the southwestern side of 
the convection, but the distance is decreasing to the mid-level 
center.  A recent scatterometer pass shows maximum winds near 50 
kt, and given the known low bias of ASCAT, the intensity is set to 
55 kt, which also matches the latest TAFB classification.
 
Karina is moving northwestward at about 9 kt.  There are no 
changes in the synoptic pattern to report as a mid-level ridge
over the SW United States should gradually build westward.  This 
evolution forces Karina to turn west-northwestward and westward this
weekend.  A bend back to the northwest is likely early next week
due to the ridge being weakened by an approaching mid-latitude 
trough.  The guidance envelope is very similar to the last forecast 
advisory, and the new forecast is close to the previous one, near 
the latest HFIP Corrected Consensus Approach (HCCA) model.

There is some increasing confidence that Karina will become a 
strong hurricane with signs of inner-core alignment ongoing.  Given 
the light shear, it seems very likely that sometime this weekend 
the low- and mid-level centers will become positioned for 
significant strengthening in otherwise conducive large-scale 
conditions.  Thus the new forecast is higher than the last one, and 
could be conservative near peak intensity given rising rapid 
intensification probabilities from SHIPS and DTOPS.  Weakening 
should begin in 4 days or so due to the cyclone moving over the 
cooling waters of the eastern Pacific.

item.title: Tropical Storm Lowell Forecast Discussion Number 4
item.description:
Issued at 500 AM HST Fri Aug 28 2026 
000
WTPZ42 KNHC 281440
TCDEP2
 
Tropical Storm Lowell Discussion Number   4
NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL       EP122026
500 AM HST Fri Aug 28 2026
 
Northeasterly to easterly vertical wind shear continues to affect
Lowell, with the low-level center currently exposed to the northeast
of the deep convection. However, a recent burst of convection has 
developed closer to the center in the last hour or so. Objective 
satellite intensity estimates from UW-CIMSS range from 33 to 40 kt, 
and the latest subjective Dvorak classification from TAFB is 
T2.5/35 kt with a Current Intensity (CI) of 3.0/45 kt. Based on a 
blend of these estimates and recent satellite trends, the initial 
intensity is held at 40 kt.
 
The initial motion remains slowly east-northeastward. This slow
motion should continue through today, followed by a gradual turn
toward the west-northwest and west tonight into tomorrow as a
mid-level ridge begins to build to the north of the cyclone. As this
ridge strengthens, the system should gradually accelerate westward.
Beyond 48 to 72 hours, considerable along- and cross-track spread
remains in the model guidance. This uncertainty is tied to the
complex evolution of multiple systems and disturbances in the
central and eastern Pacific, and their subsequent impacts on the
steering flow. The latest NHC track forecast remains on the faster
side of the guidance envelope, generally blending the faster HCCA
and slightly slower TVCN consensus aids. The Google DeepMind model
is the fastest solution provided by the guidance, however as noted
in previous discussions, this model has exhibited a fast bias in the
Pacific basin this season.
 
Although Lowell is dealing with some moderate vertical wind shear, 
environmental conditions are expected to remain or become even more 
favorable for intensification over the next several days. The 
cyclone is forecast to move over warm sea surface temperatures 
within an environment of light to moderate shear and abundant 
mid-level moisture. Particularly beyond 60 hours, the intensity 
guidance indicates steady strengthening, and the system is forecast 
to reach hurricane intensity by this weekend. The updated NHC 
intensity forecast is similar to the previous advisory, lying near 
the high end of the guidance suite in the short term and closer to 
the middle of the envelope beyond 72 hours. However, it should be 
noted that some of the regional hurricane models, and HCCA suggest a 
faster rate of intensification is possible.
